topicDisplay: D1–D2 — Continuity and change: molecules and cells
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Replication makes exact copies, and every dividing cell needs it
Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
Transcription: RNA polymerase makes an RNA copy of one gene
A DNA template can be read again and again without changing
What mRNA, the ribosome and tRNA each do
Why the code uses triplets, and what degenerate and universal mean
Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
A single base change can change a protein
Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
Mutation is random, but not evenly spread
New cells only come from cells dividing
Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
Mitosis keeps the genome; meiosis halves it and adds variety
Chromosomes condense and are moved by microtubules in both divisions
Meiosis: two divisions, one diploid nucleus to four haploid
Meiosis makes variation: random orientation and crossing over
How water dissolves ions and polar molecules
Predicting the direction of water movement for a cell
Cells with walls become turgid or plasmolyse

questions.q: A cut in the skin heals as new skin cells are produced by cell division. Why must DNA replication take place before each of these divisions?
options: So that each new cell receives a complete copy of the DNA with an identical base sequence.
So that the existing DNA can be divided equally, half going to each of the new cells.
It does not need to take place, because replication is only required for reproduction.
So that the original DNA can stay intact in one cell and the other cell gets a new copy.
optionWhy: DNA replication produces exact copies of DNA with identical base sequences. It is required not only for reproduction but for growth and tissue replacement, because every cell produced by division must receive a complete copy.
A student who thinks division shares out the DNA picks this. The DNA is copied before division so that each new cell receives a complete set, not half of the original.

A student who links replication only with reproduction picks this. Replication is also required for growth and tissue replacement in multicellular organisms, since each new cell needs a full copy of the DNA.
A student who imagines conservative replication picks this. Each daughter molecule contains one original strand and one new strand, so neither cell receives the intact original molecule.
questions.explain: DNA replication produces exact copies of DNA with identical base sequences. It is required not only for reproduction but for growth and tissue replacement, because every cell produced by division must receive a complete copy.

questions.q: What is the role of helicase in DNA replication?
options: It cuts through the sugar–phosphate backbone so that the two strands can come apart.
It adds free nucleotides to each exposed template strand to assemble the two new strands.
It forms the hydrogen bonds that hold each new nucleotide to its complementary base on the template.
It unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between the two strands.
optionWhy: A student who thinks helicase cuts the DNA picks this. Helicase breaks only the hydrogen bonds between bases; the covalent backbone of each strand stays intact so that it can act as a template.
A student who has swapped the two enzymes picks this. Assembling the new strands is the general role of DNA polymerase, not of helicase.
A student who believes an enzyme must make the base pairs picks this. Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases form spontaneously; helicase breaks hydrogen bonds rather than forming them.
Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the strands so that each can serve as a template for DNA polymerase.
questions.explain: Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the strands so that each can serve as a template for DNA polymerase.

questions.q: A forensic laboratory compares a sample from a crime scene with a suspect's DNA using 20 different markers rather than one. Why does this make the result more reliable?
options: One marker is already conclusive, because everyone's DNA is unique; extra markers only make the bands easier to read.
Testing 20 markers is equivalent to repeating a single marker 20 times, and repeating a measurement makes it more accurate.
Each extra independent marker multiplies down the chance that an unrelated person matches by coincidence.
With 20 markers the whole base sequence of the suspect's genome is read, so the identification is made complete.
optionWhy: A student who transfers the uniqueness of a whole genome to a single marker picks this. Each marker is shared by a proportion of the population, so one marker gives many chance matches.

A student who reads 'more measurements' as 'repeat the same measurement' picks this. Repeating one marker gives the same lengths each time and does not change the chance that another person shares them.

The chance that an unrelated person matches at one marker might be a few per cent; the chances at independent markers multiply together, so with 20 markers a false match becomes extremely improbable. This is the NOS principle that reliability is enhanced by increasing the number of measurements.
A student who thinks profiling reads DNA sequences picks this. A profile compares fragment lengths at a small number of variable regions; it does not read the base sequence of the genome.
questions.explain: The chance that an unrelated person matches at one marker might be a few per cent; the chances at independent markers multiply together, so with 20 markers a false match becomes extremely improbable. This is the NOS principle that reliability is enhanced by increasing the number of measurements.

questions.q: Which statement describes the roles of RNA polymerase in transcription?
options: It separates the DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides, positioned by pairing with the template strand, into one RNA strand.
It links RNA nucleotides into a strand once helicase has opened the DNA and a primer has been laid down.
It copies both DNA strands of the gene at the same time, producing a double-stranded RNA molecule from the gene.
It joins amino acids together, one after another, in the order specified by the base sequence of the gene.
optionWhy: RNA polymerase binds to the gene, separates the DNA strands, positions free RNA nucleotides by complementary base pairing with the template strand and forms the covalent bonds that join them into a single RNA strand.

A student who transfers the replication machinery to transcription picks this. RNA polymerase separates the DNA strands itself and needs no primer; helicase and primase are not involved in transcription.
A student who models transcription on replication picks this. Only one strand, the template strand, is transcribed, and the product is a single strand of RNA.
A student who has swapped transcription and translation picks this. Amino acids are joined during translation on a ribosome; RNA polymerase joins RNA nucleotides, not amino acids.
questions.explain: RNA polymerase binds to the gene, separates the DNA strands, positions free RNA nucleotides by complementary base pairing with the template strand and forms the covalent bonds that join them into a single RNA strand.

questions.q: A neuron formed before birth does not divide again, yet it transcribes the same genes throughout a lifetime of many decades. Which statement explains how this is possible?
options: Each round of transcription slightly alters the template, so the neuron periodically replicates its DNA to restore the gene.
Because the neuron does not replicate its DNA again, its base sequences need not be conserved and can change freely.
Transcription copies both strands of the gene just as replication does, so every round of transcription renews the gene.
Transcription reads the template strand without altering its base sequence, so the sequence is conserved for life.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a template wears out picks this. The template is read by base pairing and left unchanged, and a non-dividing neuron does not replicate its DNA at all.
A student who thinks DNA matters only when copied picks this. The neuron's DNA is the template for all its transcription, so a changed sequence would change every transcript for the rest of its life.

A student who models transcription on replication picks this. Only the template strand is transcribed, into single-stranded RNA; the gene persists because transcription does not change it, not because it is re-copied.

A single DNA strand can be used as a template for transcription without its base sequence changing. In a somatic cell that does not divide, the sequences are conserved and reused for the life of the cell.
questions.explain: A single DNA strand can be used as a template for transcription without its base sequence changing. In a somatic cell that does not divide, the sequences are conserved and reused for the life of the cell.

questions.q: Which statement about the binding of mRNA and tRNA to a ribosome is correct?
options: The mRNA binds to the large subunit, because it is the larger molecule, and the tRNAs bind to the small subunit.
The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and only one tRNA can bind to the large subunit at any moment.
The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and every tRNA needed for the polypeptide binds along it at once.
The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and two tRNAs can bind to the large subunit at the same time.
optionWhy: A student who matches molecule size to subunit size picks this. It is the small subunit that binds the mRNA; the tRNA binding sites are on the large subunit.
A student who pictures one tRNA delivering at a time picks this. Two tRNAs bind simultaneously, so the amino acid on the new tRNA can be joined to the chain held by the other.
A student who takes diagrams of several tRNAs literally picks this. Only two tRNAs are bound at a time, and the ribosome works along the mRNA stepwise.

mRNA binds to the small subunit of the ribosome, and two tRNAs can bind simultaneously to the large subunit, allowing a peptide bond to form between the amino acid on one and the polypeptide on the other.
questions.explain: mRNA binds to the small subunit of the ribosome, and two tRNAs can bind simultaneously to the large subunit, allowing a peptide bond to form between the amino acid on one and the polypeptide on the other.

questions.q: Why does the genetic code use codons of three bases rather than two?
options: Two bases would give 16 codons, which is close enough to 20 for nearly all the amino acids to be coded.
Three bases allow each codon to code for up to three different amino acids whenever these are needed.
Three bases give 64 possible codons, enough for 20 amino acids, whereas two bases give only 16.
Three bases let the ribosome start reading at any point, since any group of three is a codon.
optionWhy: A student who has not seen the constraint picks this. Sixteen codons cannot specify 20 amino acids; every amino acid needs at least one codon of its own.
A student who thinks the code is ambiguous picks this. Each codon specifies only one amino acid; the number of bases sets how many different codons exist, not how many amino acids one codon can mean.

With four bases, two-base codons give 4 × 4 = 16 combinations, fewer than the 20 amino acids used in polypeptides. Three-base codons give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, more than enough, so a triplet code is the shortest that works.

A student without a fixed reading frame picks this. Codons are read in a fixed frame from the start codon, and reading from another base gives a wrong sequence; the triplet length is about having enough codons.
questions.explain: With four bases, two-base codons give 4 × 4 = 16 combinations, fewer than the 20 amino acids used in polypeptides. Three-base codons give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, more than enough, so a triplet code is the shortest that works.

questions.q: Part of an mRNA molecule, written in the order in which it is translated, has the base sequence AUGGGCAACAGA. The genetic code table gives: AUG methionine, GGC glycine, AAC asparagine, AGA arginine, UAC tyrosine, CCG proline, UUG leucine, UCU serine, UGG tryptophan, GCA alanine, ACA threonine. Which amino acid is the third in the polypeptide?
options: arginine
asparagine
leucine
threonine
optionWhy: A student who treats AUG as a start signal only, and begins counting from GGC, makes arginine (AGA) the third amino acid. AUG codes for methionine, which is the first amino acid, so the third is asparagine.
Reading from the start codon in groups of three gives AUG GGC AAC AGA: methionine, glycine, asparagine, arginine. The third codon, AAC, codes for asparagine.

A student who first writes the complementary sequence (UAC CCG UUG UCU) and looks that up picks leucine. The table is for mRNA codons and the sequence given is already mRNA, so no complement should be taken.
A student who begins reading from the second base (UGG GCA ACA) picks threonine. The reading frame is fixed by the start codon AUG, so codons must be counted from the first base.
questions.explain: Reading from the start codon in groups of three gives AUG GGC AAC AGA: methionine, glycine, asparagine, arginine. The third codon, AAC, codes for asparagine.

questions.q: A base substitution in a gene changes an mRNA codon from GGU to GGC. Both codons code for glycine. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
options: Its structure changes, because a different codon is bound to give a different amino acid.
Every amino acid after this point changes, because the reading frame has been shifted.
There is no effect, because the same amino acid, glycine, is inserted at that position.
Glycine may be replaced, because GGC can also code for a different amino acid.
optionWhy: A student who expects every substitution to change the protein picks this. Degeneracy means a changed codon can still specify the same amino acid, as here.
A student who thinks all point mutations shift the frame picks this. A substitution replaces one base with another and leaves the reading frame intact.
Because the genetic code is degenerate, GGU and GGC both code for glycine. The polypeptide's amino acid sequence, and so its structure, is unchanged by this silent substitution.
A student who thinks the code is ambiguous picks this. Each codon specifies one amino acid only; GGC always codes for glycine.
questions.explain: Because the genetic code is degenerate, GGU and GGC both code for glycine. The polypeptide's amino acid sequence, and so its structure, is unchanged by this silent substitution.

questions.q: Why is a polypeptide likely to cease functioning when several hundred bases are deleted from the middle of its gene?
options: Only because a deletion of any size shifts the reading frame of every later codon
So many amino acids are missing that the polypeptide cannot fold into its working shape
Only the amino acids coded by the deleted bases are missing; the rest still folds as normal
The amino acids coded before the deletion are also changed by the loss of bases
optionWhy: A student who thinks every deletion is a frameshift picks this. If the number of bases deleted is a multiple of three the frame is unchanged, yet the polypeptide still loses many amino acids and is likely to cease to function for that reason.

A major deletion removes a large section of the coding sequence, so a long run of amino acids is absent from the polypeptide. Even if the reading frame happens to be preserved, a polypeptide missing so much of its sequence is unlikely to fold into a functional shape.

A student who assumes the effect of a deletion is confined to the mutation point, as for a single-base change, picks this. Several hundred bases code for a hundred or more amino acids (three bases per amino acid), and losing that much of the sequence prevents the polypeptide from folding into its functional shape, even if the reading frame is preserved.

A student who thinks any change spreads back along the polypeptide picks this. Codons before the deletion are read exactly as before; the damage lies in the large section that is missing and, if the frame is shifted, in the sequence after it.
questions.explain: A major deletion removes a large section of the coding sequence, so a long run of amino acids is absent from the polypeptide. Even if the reading frame happens to be preserved, a polypeptide missing so much of its sequence is unlikely to fold into a functional shape.

questions.q: Which statement about randomness in mutation is correct?
options: Mutations can occur anywhere in the genome, but some bases have a higher probability of mutating than others
Mutations can occur anywhere in the genome, and every base has an identical probability of mutating
Mutations occur in the genes an organism needs to change when its environment changes
Mutations occur only at those bases in the genome that a mutagen has chemically damaged
optionWhy: Mutation is random in the sense that no natural mechanism directs a change to a particular base for the purpose of changing a trait; it is not uniform, because the chemistry of some bases and sequences (for example methylated cytosine) makes them mutation hotspots.
A student who reads random as equally likely picks this. Randomness refers to the lack of direction towards a useful outcome; some bases mutate much more often than others.
A student who thinks organisms mutate in response to need picks this. No natural mechanism is known for making a deliberate change to a particular base with the purpose of changing a trait.
A student who ties every mutation to a mutagen picks this. Errors in replication or repair cause mutations at bases that no mutagen has touched, anywhere in the genome.
questions.explain: Mutation is random in the sense that no natural mechanism directs a change to a particular base for the purpose of changing a trait; it is not uniform, because the chemistry of some bases and sequences (for example methylated cytosine) makes them mutation hotspots.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how new cells are generated in a living organism?
options: A parent cell divides to produce two daughter cells, and everything the parent contained is shared out between them.
A parent cell produces two daughter cells and then goes on living alongside them as a third cell.
A parent cell splits at one moment into many small daughter cells, which then grow to full size in the tissue.
A parent cell splits its cytoplasm into two halves, each of which then assembles a nucleus of its own from the cytoplasm.
optionWhy: In all living organisms new cells arise by division of a parent (mother) cell into two daughter cells. The parent cell does not persist; its whole contents are divided between the two daughters.
A student who reads 'mother' and 'daughter' as a human family picks this. The parent cell is the material from which the two daughter cells are made; no third cell remains.
A student who pictures one cell fragmenting into many picks this. Each division produces exactly two daughter cells; large numbers come from repeated divisions.
A student who thinks a nucleus can be built from scratch picks this. The nucleus divides first by mitosis or meiosis, and each daughter cell receives one of the two nuclei produced.
questions.explain: In all living organisms new cells arise by division of a parent (mother) cell into two daughter cells. The parent cell does not persist; its whole contents are divided between the two daughters.

questions.q: Which statement about the division of the cytoplasm between two daughter cells is correct?
options: The cytoplasm is divided equally in every cell division, so that each daughter cell receives exactly half of each type of organelle.
A daughter cell that receives no mitochondria can synthesize new ones from proteins made on its ribosomes, so none need be shared.
When cytoplasm is divided unequally, the daughter cell that receives more cytoplasm also receives the larger share of the chromosomes.
Each daughter cell must receive at least one mitochondrion, because mitochondria form only by division of existing ones.
optionWhy: A student who has only seen symmetrical diagrams picks this. Division of the cytoplasm is usually equal but not in all cases; oogenesis and yeast budding are unequal.
A student who thinks a cell can build any structure from raw materials picks this. Mitochondria arise only from existing mitochondria, which is exactly why each daughter must receive at least one.
A student who equates the size of a cell with its share of everything picks this. The chromosomes are shared equally by nuclear division; only the cytoplasm is divided unequally.
Mitochondria, like chloroplasts, can only be made by division of a pre-existing organelle. A daughter cell that received none could not make any, so at least one must be passed to each cell.
questions.explain: Mitochondria, like chloroplasts, can only be made by division of a pre-existing organelle. A daughter cell that received none could not make any, so at least one must be passed to each cell.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the roles of mitosis and meiosis in eukaryotes?
options: Mitosis keeps the full set of genes in each cell, whereas meiosis produces cells that carry only half of the organism's genes.
Mitosis keeps the chromosome number and genome of the cell the same, whereas meiosis halves the chromosome number and generates diversity.
Mitosis doubles the chromosome number, which meiosis then halves, so together the two processes keep the number constant.
Mitosis separates the two chromosomes of each homologous pair into different cells, whereas meiosis separates the sister chromatids.
optionWhy: A student who hears 'halves the chromosome number' as 'halves the genes' picks this. A haploid nucleus has one chromosome of every pair and so one copy of every gene.
Mitosis maintains the chromosome number and genome of cells, producing genetically identical nuclei. Meiosis halves the chromosome number and generates genetic diversity among the nuclei it produces.
A student who thinks replication or mitosis doubles the chromosome number picks this. Mitosis maintains the number; it is fertilization that doubles it and meiosis that halves it.
A student who transfers the separation of homologues from meiosis to mitosis picks this. Mitosis separates sister chromatids, so both members of every pair go to each daughter cell.
questions.explain: Mitosis maintains the chromosome number and genome of cells, producing genetically identical nuclei. Meiosis halves the chromosome number and generates genetic diversity among the nuclei it produces.

questions.q: How is the DNA of a eukaryotic chromosome condensed before nuclear division?
options: The double helix itself twists ever more tightly, with no proteins involved, until the molecule is short enough to be seen.
The DNA is wound around histone proteins, and the fibre so formed is supercoiled into a much shorter, thicker structure.
The DNA is already packed as a condensed chromosome throughout the cycle; staining at division merely makes it visible.
The DNA is copied, and the two new copies pack tightly against each other to form the short, visible chromosome.
optionWhy: A student who hears 'supercoiling' as more of the helix's own coiling picks this. The naked helix cannot be packed into a chromosome; the coiling is of DNA wound around histone proteins.
Condensation depends on histones: DNA wound around histones forms nucleosomes, and the DNA–protein fibre is then coiled and supercoiled, shortening the chromosome so it can be moved without tangling.
A student who takes the karyotype image as the permanent state of DNA picks this. Between divisions the DNA is extended for transcription and replication; it condenses only for nuclear division.
A student who confuses replication with condensation picks this. Replication happens in interphase and produces two chromatids; it is supercoiling around histones, not copying, that shortens them.
questions.explain: Condensation depends on histones: DNA wound around histones forms nucleosomes, and the DNA–protein fibre is then coiled and supercoiled, shortening the chromosome so it can be moved without tangling.

questions.q: Which statement correctly outlines the two rounds of segregation in meiosis?
options: In meiosis I the two chromosomes of each homologous pair separate; in meiosis II the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate.
In meiosis I the sister chromatids of each chromosome are separated, and in meiosis II the homologous chromosomes of each pair are separated.
In meiosis I the homologous chromosomes are separated; the DNA is then replicated so that meiosis II can separate the new chromatids.
In meiosis I each chromosome is split into its maternal chromatid and its paternal chromatid, and meiosis II shares these between nuclei.
optionWhy: Meiosis I is the reduction division: the two chromosomes of each bivalent go to opposite poles, so each nucleus has one chromosome of every pair. Meiosis II separates the two chromatids of each of those chromosomes.
A student who assumes the first division is 'the same as mitosis' picks this. The order is the reverse: homologues separate first, chromatids second.
A student who applies 'replicate then divide' to each division picks this. No replication occurs between the divisions; the chromatids separated in meiosis II were made before meiosis I.
A student who thinks the two chromatids come from the two parents picks this. Sister chromatids are identical copies; the maternal and paternal chromosomes are the two members of a homologous pair.
questions.explain: Meiosis I is the reduction division: the two chromosomes of each bivalent go to opposite poles, so each nucleus has one chromosome of every pair. Meiosis II separates the two chromatids of each of those chromosomes.

questions.q: Which statement about crossing over is correct?
options: Sister chromatids of one chromosome exchange lengths of DNA, so that the two chromatids come to differ from each other.
The exchange of DNA alters the base sequence at the exchanged region, creating new alleles of the genes found there.
The exchange between chromatids decides which chromosome of each pair moves to each pole of the cell in anaphase I.
Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange lengths of DNA, producing new combinations of alleles.
optionWhy: A student who remembers 'chromatids exchange segments' without 'non-sister' picks this. Sister chromatids are identical, so exchanging DNA between them could produce no new combination.
A student who confuses new combinations with new alleles picks this. Crossing over exchanges existing alleles between homologues; new alleles arise only by mutation.
A student who merges crossing over with random orientation picks this. Which homologue goes to which pole is decided by the random orientation of the bivalent at metaphase I, a separate process.

Crossing over occurs in prophase I, while homologous chromosomes are paired as a bivalent. Non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding lengths of DNA, so each chromatid carries a new combination of the alleles present on the two homologues.
questions.explain: Crossing over occurs in prophase I, while homologous chromosomes are paired as a bivalent. Non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding lengths of DNA, so each chromatid carries a new combination of the alleles present on the two homologues.

questions.q: Sodium chloride dissolves when it is placed in water. Which statement describes the attractions that hold the ions in solution?
options: Na⁺ ions are attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of water molecules, and Cl⁻ ions to the partially positive hydrogen atoms.
Hydrogen bonds form between each ion and the water molecules that surround it, just as they form between water molecules.
Both kinds of ion are attracted to the oxygen end of the water molecules, because that is the end that carries a charge.
Water molecules react chemically with the sodium chloride, breaking it down into separate sodium and chlorine atoms.
optionWhy: Water is polar. Each positively charged Na⁺ ion is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of surrounding water molecules, and each negatively charged Cl⁻ ion to the partially positive hydrogen atoms, so the ions are separated and held in solution.

A student who uses hydrogen bonding to explain every property of water picks this. Hydrogen bonds form between water and polar molecules such as glucose; an ion is held in solution by the attraction between its charge and the partial charges on water.

A student who has only seen a hydrated sodium ion drawn picks this. The hydrogen atoms of water carry partial positive charges, so it is the hydrogen end that is attracted to a negatively charged chloride ion.
A student who thinks of dissolving as a chemical change picks this. No reaction occurs: the ions stay as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and are simply separated and surrounded by water molecules.
questions.explain: Water is polar. Each positively charged Na⁺ ion is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of surrounding water molecules, and each negatively charged Cl⁻ ion to the partially positive hydrogen atoms, so the ions are separated and held in solution.

questions.q: A cell is placed in a solution that is isotonic with its cytoplasm. Which statement describes the movement of water across its membrane?
options: Water molecules cross the membrane in both directions at equal rates, so there is a dynamic equilibrium with no net movement.
Water molecules stop crossing the membrane in either direction, because there is no concentration gradient to drive them.
Solute molecules cross the membrane in both directions, keeping the concentrations on the two sides of the membrane equal.
The cell stops pumping water across the membrane, because it no longer needs to use energy to adjust its water content.
optionWhy: In an isotonic environment water molecules continue to enter and leave the cell, but at the same rate. This is a dynamic equilibrium: there is no net movement of water, not an absence of movement.
A student who drops the word 'net' picks this. Individual water molecules move randomly through the membrane whatever the concentrations; the gradient only decides whether there is a net direction.

A student who thinks of concentration differences as being managed by the solute picks this. The membrane is partially permeable, and the question concerns water, which crosses in both directions at equal rates.
A student who believes the cell actively controls osmosis picks this. Osmosis is passive and uses no energy; water crosses the membrane continuously in both directions in an isotonic solution.
questions.explain: In an isotonic environment water molecules continue to enter and leave the cell, but at the same rate. This is a dynamic equilibrium: there is no net movement of water, not an absence of movement.

questions.q: A strip of onion epidermis is mounted in a concentrated sucrose solution and viewed under a microscope. Which statement describes what happens to its cells?
options: Water leaves each cell by osmosis and the whole cell, wall included, shrinks and crumples inward, just as an animal cell crenates.
Water leaves each cell by osmosis and an empty space forms between the wall and the membrane, because the wall lets nothing through.
Water leaves each cell by osmosis, the protoplast shrinks and its membrane pulls away from the wall: the cells are plasmolysed.
Water enters each cell by osmosis, because the concentrated solution is hypotonic to them, and the cells become turgid.
optionWhy: A student who transfers crenation to plant cells picks this. The rigid cellulose wall keeps its shape; only the protoplast inside it shrinks.
A student who treats the wall as a barrier picks this. The cell wall is freely permeable, so the space that opens up is filled by the sucrose solution.

The concentrated sucrose solution is hypertonic to the cell sap, so water leaves by osmosis. The protoplast shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall, which keeps its shape: this is plasmolysis.
A student who has swapped hypo- and hyper- picks this. A concentrated solution has the higher solute concentration, so it is hypertonic and water leaves the cells.
questions.explain: The concentrated sucrose solution is hypertonic to the cell sap, so water leaves by osmosis. The protoplast shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall, which keeps its shape: this is plasmolysis.
